stages.sub: Why swapping goods breaks down, and the four jobs money does to fix it.

steps.q: A farmer who grows only wheat wants a pair of shoes. The shoemaker does not want any wheat, only fish. Can they swap directly?
steps.right: No, each would need to want the other's goods
steps.wrong: Yes, any two goods can always be swapped
steps.hint: A swap only works if each side wants exactly what the other has.

steps.q: Without money, most people cannot find someone who wants what they have and has what they want. What happens to trade?
steps.right: It shrinks, as most swaps keep failing
steps.wrong: It grows, as swaps become easier
steps.hint: How often would you find a perfect match every time you wanted something?

steps.q: To get round failed swaps, the farmer and shoemaker need something any seller will accept. What would that be?
steps.wrong: Only fish, since most people want fish
steps.hint: It must not be tied to any one person's wants.

steps.right: The shoes are worth 20 times as much as the bread
steps.wrong: You cannot compare them without seeing both items

steps.q: You earn £500 and don't spend it all. Can you still buy things with the rest in six months, if prices barely change?
steps.right: Yes, it keeps its worth until you spend it
steps.wrong: No, unspent money loses its usefulness after a while
steps.hint: Does money disappear or rot if you hold on to it rather than spending it straight away?

steps.q: You buy a sofa today and pay in three monthly instalments. Can money settle a debt for something bought now, paid later?
steps.right: Yes, you can agree to pay the value later
steps.wrong: No, payment must always happen at the moment of the sale
steps.hint: The sofa is delivered today, but the full payment happens over future months.
